title: Israeli strikes kill 11 in southern Lebanese village, including two infants
summary:
Israeli strikes kill 11 in southern Lebanese village, including two infants

Submitted by MEE staff on Mon, 09/07/2026 - 10:00
Nine people die as residential building is destroyed in Kfar Rumman, while a separate drone strike kills two paramedics
A Lebanese army soldier inspects destroyed vehicles at the site of an overnight Israeli air strike on the village of Kfar Rumman in southern Lebanon on 7 September 2026 (Mahmoud Zayyat/AFP)
Off

Israeli strikes killed 11 people in the southern Lebanese town of Kfar Rumman overnight, including two infants, Lebanese state media reported on Monday.

Nine people were killed and five others wounded when an Israeli strike destroyed a three-storey residential building in the town, according to Lebanon’s official National News Agency (NNA).

A separate Israeli drone strike hit a vehicle in Kfar Rumman, killing two paramedics identified as Ali Shahrour and Hadi Farhat. The pair worked for the Islamic Scout Association, the NNA reported.

Rescue workers were still searching the ruins of the residential building for possible survivors and additional victims on Monday morning.

Photographs from the scene showed the building reduced to rubble, with schoolbooks and pieces of furniture scattered among the debris. Nearby buildings were also damaged, prompting some residents to flee, AFP reported.

Kfar Rumman lies close to the major southern city of Nabatieh. Residents had returned to the town following the June truce after previously being displaced by the war.

Israel did not issue an evacuation warning ahead of the strikes on Kfar Rumman.

However, its military issued a warning before carrying out a separate attack on a building in nearby Deir Zahrani, saying it was targeting a Hezbollah facility.

The NNA said the building was destroyed 22 minutes after the warning was issued.

The Israeli military said an explosive-laden drone had been launched towards its forces, without specifying whether there had been any casualties. It said Hezbollah’s activities had compelled it to respond forcefully.

Fighting intensifies

The latest fighting began on 2 March, when Hezbollah launched attacks on Israel in what it described as retaliation for the killing of Iran’s supreme leader and repeated Israeli violations of the previous ceasefire. Israel responded with strikes across Lebanon.

Lebanon’s health ministry said on Sunday that Israeli attacks had killed 4,362 people and wounded 12,378 since the conflict began.

The fighting subsided after a June memorandum of understanding between Washington and Tehran concerning the wider regional war, followed by an agreement between Israel and Lebanon later that month.

Israel has nevertheless continued to bomb Lebanon and occupy parts of its territory despite a ceasefire that took effect on 17 April and was renewed on 26 June.

Hezbollah's Nawaf Moussawi: Only force can compel Israel to leave Lebanon
Read More »

Israeli forces remain deployed in a self-declared buffer zone extending about 10km into southern Lebanon. Amnesty International said in June that the zone covered approximately six percent of the country.

Israeli strikes on Sunday killed at least seven people, including two women, and wounded 20 others.

Israel has intensified its attacks around Nabatieh since announcing on Thursday that it had seized the strategically located Ali al-Taher ridge from Hezbollah, a claim the group hasn't officially commented on. 

Israel has accused Hezbollah of repeatedly violating the ceasefire and attempting to rebuild its military capabilities in southern Lebanon.

“Repeated drone attacks. Weapons storage. Terror infrastructure. Command centres embedded in civilian areas,” Israel’s foreign ministry wrote on X on Monday. “These violations will not be accepted.”

The ceasefire agreement includes provisions for Hezbollah’s disarmament.

On Sunday, Lebanese President Joseph Aoun urged the US and the international community to intervene to halt Israel’s attacks.

Aoun described the strikes, which damaged government premises and destroyed an out-of-service hospital, as “a dangerous escalation” that had reached Lebanese state institutions and health facilities.

He called on Washington and other governments “to urgently act to stop these violations”.

title: Ed Miliband is tearing up the script to become the UK's most formidable foreign secretary in decades
summary:
Ed Miliband is tearing up the script to become the UK's most formidable foreign secretary in decades

Submitted by Peter Oborne on Mon, 09/07/2026 - 10:50
The settlement goods ban looks set to be seismic - a sign that Britain has the makings of a new, independent foreign policy
Britain's Foreign Secretary Ed Miliband poses during a meeting with his French counterpart at the Quai d'Orsay in Paris on 29 July (AFP)
Off

Rarely has a British foreign secretary come under such ferocious attack as Ed Miliband over the past weeks.

Miliband provoked a two-pronged assault when he announced his intention to impose punitive measures against Israel in an attempt to halt settler violence - and rescue the prospect of a Palestinian state.

The foreign secretary is set to announce a ban on trade with illegal Israeli settlements on Tuesday. The ban will aim to bring the UK into compliance with the International Court of Justice’s advisory opinion of July 2024, according to Whitehall sources.

Many pro-Palestine advocates complain that Miliband's statement comes far too late, will not go nearly far enough and in any case will consist of largely meaningless gestures.

They are further angered by Labour's refusal to employ the term genocide, halt all arms sales to Israel and sanction Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu.

The American and Israeli responses to Miliband's plans, however, have been brutal.

In a highly unusual diplomatic intervention, US Ambassador to Israel Mike Huckabee posted on X on Saturday: "The Brits have lost it.  The Jew hate of their government knows no boundaries and knows no facts."

Miliband is ethnically Jewish and Huckabee is not.

Netanyahu last month branded Britain the "Islamic Republic of Britain".

The Israeli government's outrage is accompanied by threats. "If Britain acts against Israel, Israel will act against Britain," warned the Israeli Foreign Minister Gideon Saar last week. 

How Israel armed Argentina to kill British soldiers during Falklands War
Read More »

Yair Netanyahu, son of the prime minister, declared that the Falkland Islands belongs to Argentina, not Britain.

US President Donald Trump then suggested he would not back the UK if Argentina invaded the territory.

The Tory opposition, heavily backed by the British right-wing press, has echoed this vociferous criticism.

The Sunday Telegraph awarded massive prominence to an interview with the new shadow foreign secretary, Tom Tugendhat. Tugendhat took the side of Israel against the British government and cited Israeli threats that British national security could be threatened if Britain sanctions the settlements.

The advocacy group Conservative Friends of Israel has moreover accused Miliband of planning "a morally indefensible move that further singles out and demonises the world's only Jewish state and a close ally."

Miliband is stepping out of line

The British foreign secretary, who has been in office for just two months, is showing unusual determination amid the onslaught of threats and criticism.

No foreign secretary this century has ever successfully challenged either the power of the White House or pressure from Israel – let alone both at once. 

Miliband is stepping out of line. Moreover, he is doing so against strident opposition from significant sections of the British media. In short, Miliband has torn up the script on British foreign policy.

Mike Huckabee criticised for accusing Jewish UK foreign secretary of 'Jew hate'
Read More »

In his first performance as foreign secretary in parliament last Tuesday, he promised a "comprehensive reset" of policy on Israel. Miliband insisted Britain "will not acquiesce in the destruction of the two-state solution."

He assured Labour, Green and SNP MPs who pressed him to act against Israel's settlement expansion in the occupied West Bank that they wouldn’t have to wait much longer.

Well-informed sources tell Middle East Eye that, inside the Burnham government, Miliband has been the internal driving force behind the policies he is expected to announce on Tuesday.

The foreign secretary has also deployed a new language on Gaza: "I just came out of this meeting talking about Gaza to people who've been there and are there on the ground, and frankly it was horrific what is unfolding."

He asserted last week that "we as a UK government, as the prime minister has said, have got to act and act more decisively than we have."

His two predecessors as Labour foreign secretary, David Lammy and Yvette Cooper, will each have been given horrifying briefings on conditions in Gaza. 

Neither reacted in the strong and anguished way that Miliband has chosen to do.

These words mark him out as an unusually moral and humane politician.

Almost as significant, the force of his language means that it will be impossible for Miliband to give in to future US and Israeli pressure without opening himself to charges of hypocrisy. 

Settlement goods ban set to be seismic

These developments come at a pivotal moment. Israel's new E1 settlement project east of Jerusalem is poised to effectively cut the occupied West Bank in two. It is designed to make a Palestinian state completely unviable.

Britain’s settlement goods ban therefore looks set to be seismic. As Ben Jamal, until recently the director of the Palestine Solidarity Campaign, recently put it: "Such a ban has been a core demand of the Palestine solidarity movement for many years, as a key basic step towards ending UK complicity with Israel’s violations of international law."

A report that Netanyahu is already ordering the removal of settler outposts, if confirmed, would suggest that Britain's stand could be having an immediate effect

If properly implemented, the ban will bring the UK into compliance with the 2024 ICJ advisory opinion, which declared the Israeli occupation of Palestinian territory to be illegal and obligated states - including Britain - to take steps to oppose it.

To achieve this, the ban will need to be comprehensive and cover both goods and services. It will have to prohibit any investment in settlement businesses and be backed up by real enforcement powers.

Other European countries, including Ireland, Spain and Belgium, have introduced similar measures. But Whitehall sources insist the UK’s planned sanctions will be even stronger.

While it is true that the ban will enrage the Netanyahu government and offend Donald Trump, it may also be a diplomatic boon for Andy Burnham's government, establishing it on the world stage as a country willing to defy the United States. 

And if Sunday's report that Netanyahu is already ordering the removal of settler outposts is confirmed, this would suggest that Britain's stand could be having an immediate effect.

Politically secure and in tune with the public

Pro-Israel critics of Miliband repeatedly accuse him of bowing to Muslim opinion in Britain. Polling does not support this claim.

Miliband's approach is, in fact, bringing foreign policy back into line with British public opinion in general. Only 16 percent of Britons, a small minority, oppose a ban on settlement goods. 

This helps to explain why more than 140 Labour backbenchers have urged the government to implement a comprehensive trade ban with the settlements.

Miliband calls Gaza situation ‘horrific’, says UK must act more decisively
Read More »

Polling of Labour members earlier this year showed that a staggering 87 percent support a ban.

This means Miliband is politically secure and in tune with the public mood. Crucially, he appears to have Downing Street's backing.

But Labour insiders stress the foreign secretary also sincerely believes these measures are necessary.

Consider his record on the issue. As Labour leader when the party was in opposition, Miliband distinguished himself by strongly criticising the coalition government's failure to challenge Israel when it bombed Gaza in 2014, killing 1,600 Palestinian civilians, including 550 children. By contast, six Israeli civilians were killed.

In 2014 Miliband accused then-Prime Minister David Cameron of getting it “wrong” and slammed his "inexplicable silence" on “the killing of innocent Palestinian civilians caused by Israel’s military action”. 

That same year, Miliband backed recognising Palestinian statehood unilaterally, a position opposed by the Tories.

In the cabinet last year, sources say, Miliband was a leading voice pressuring then-Prime Minister Keir Starmer to recognise a Palestinian state - which he finally did in September last year. 

According to a senior Whitehall source, Miliband and Home Secretary Shabana Mahmood privately lobbied Starmer not to back the US-Israeli strikes on Iran this February. 

The makings of an independent foreign policy

It is worth remembering just how significantly British foreign policy appears to have changed. Rishi Sunak's Tory government showed contempt for international law in late 2023 and early 2024. 

It publicly mocked the International Court of Justice ruling on the genocide case brought against Israel by South Africa, while Foreign Secretary David Cameron privately tried to influence the International Criminal Court’s chief prosecutor not to seek arrest warrants for Israeli ministers.

Under Starmer, two Labour foreign secretaries - Lammy and Cooper - introduced a series of half-measures against Israel.

There was an arms embargo, but not a full one. Intelligence sharing from surveillance flights over Gaza continued throughout Israel’s genocide.

When Lammy suggested Israel had broken international law, Downing Street swiftly rowed back on the comments. There was advice against businesses investing in Israeli settlements, but no ban. 

If Burnham and Miliband want to avoid the ire of the Trump administration they will need to weaken the planned sanctions. This will signal to the US and Israel that it is fundamentally business as usual, and there is no substantive change in approach from that of the Starmer government.

But if Burnham and Miliband press on with introducing and implementing the sanctions, they will be standing up to the US and Israel and announcing to the world that Britain finally has the makings of an independent foreign policy.

Analysis
Imran Mulla

title: Gaza death toll reaches 73,658 as Israeli attacks continue
summary:
Gaza death toll reaches 73,658 as Israeli attacks continue

Palestinian news agency Wafa reported that at least eight Palestinians were killed and 30 were wounded in Israeli strikes in the Gaza Strip in the past 24 hours. Two others were killed from wounds inflicted in earlier Israeli attacks. 

A Palestinian man, Ismail Ibrahim Qandil, was killed when an Israeli air strike targeted him while he was riding his motorbike northwest of Khan Younis, Wafa reported.

According to Gaza’s health ministry, since October 2023 Israel has killed at least 73,658 Palestinians and wounded 174,622 others in Gaza. 

Israeli forces also continued attacks and raids throughout Gaza and the occupied West Bank, as Israeli naval forces opened fire at fishing boats off Gaza City, wounding two fishermen. 

Israeli forces also detained Palestinians in raids in Ramallah, Tulkarm, Nilin and Nablus, while settlers attacked a farming shed, damaged electricity poles and assaulted two Palestinians south of Nablus. 

Settlers have also started fencing off land in al-Hadidiya in the Jordan Valley, restricting Palestinians’ access to agricultural areas.

An off-the-shelf VM is not enough to contain a modern, cyber-capable AI agent. There is simply too much attack surface. Even innocuous features (like running with a display) add extra, exploitable attack surface.

title: Security Vulnerability in a Voting System
summary:
It’s a vulnerability that allows someone to recover the order of ballots cast, newly exploited with AI tools.

Nearly four years since the original vulnerability was disclosed, I was still able to use it to analyze voter behavior in Georgia (one of the 21 states that uses affected scanners) in the recent May 2026 primary.

Notably, I never touched a voting machine, exploited a network, examined source code, or accessed anything non-public.

After pointing a coding agent to the original vulnerability paper, I supplied it with two data sources highlighted in the paper: the early-voting list for each county, and the “CVR” (cast-vote record) file, containing every ballot and its selections (but not the voters’ names or other identifying information). The CVR file is available upon request, precisely because a public, ballot-level record is what makes election results independently verifiable...

title: UK set to announce ban on trade with Israeli settlements on Tuesday
summary:
UK set to announce ban on trade with Israeli settlements on Tuesday

Submitted by Imran Mulla on Mon, 09/07/2026 - 09:51
New measures are expected to prohibit any investment in illegal Israeli settlement businesses
Britain's Prime Minister Andy Burnham speaks to the media after attending a preview event for the Bayeux Tapestry Exhibition, at the British Museum in London on 2 September (AFP)
Off

British Foreign Secretary Ed Miliband is set to announce a ban on trade with illegal Israeli settlements on Tuesday, Middle East Eye understands.

The ban is expected to bring the UK into compliance with the International Court of Justice’s advisory opinion of July 2024, Whitehall sources told MEE.

The ICJ ruling declared the Israeli occupation of Palestinian territory to be illegal and obligated states - including Britain - to take steps to oppose it.

To achieve this, the ban is expected to prohibit any investment in settlement businesses.

Francesca Albanese, the UN’s special rapporteur on the occupied territories, said on Monday that "all states carry an obligation - not a preference of an obligation - not to recognise the situation as legal, and not render aid and assistance in maintaining it".

Albanese said a settlement trade ban must be part of "a true paradigm shift to Israel-Palestine that ultimately seeks to implement the International Court of Justice advisory opinion in 2024".

The Labour Muslim Network (LMN) and International Centre of Justice for Palestinians (ICJP) published a legal briefing last week saying the UK should implement a "full ban on British citizens and businesses conducting economic and financial activities in illegal Israeli settlements as well as in activities that assist the wider illegal settlement economy".

The briefing said: "The legal framework governing the settlements is firmly established in international humanitarian law, including treaties to which the UK is a party.

"The UK is required not only to respect international humanitarian law but also, under Common Article 1 of the Geneva Conventions, to ensure respect for it in all circumstances."

This comes as Israel’s new E1 settlement project east of Jerusalem is poised to effectively cut the occupied West Bank in two.

Last week the Israeli government threatened Britain with retaliation over the expected measures. "If Britain acts against Israel, Israel will act against Britain," foreign minister Gideon Saar warned.

US pressure increases

Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu's son, Yair Netanyahu, suggested last week that the Falkland Islands belonged to Argentina and not to Britain. 

Yair is not a minister, but after his comments, US President Donald Trump indicated that Washington could reconsider its position on British sovereignty over the islands.

Last Thursday, Trump suggested he would not back Britain if Argentina were to invade the Falkland Islands, telling GB News: "Your country was not there to help me" when the US and Israel began their attack on Iran in February.

Argentinian President Javier Milei declared last week that Argentina's national sovereignty had been "violated" and that his country would defend its interests "tooth and nail, no matter who it bothers".

On Friday morning in a national address, Milei threatened sanctions on oil firms that seek to drill around the Falklands, adding that the "winds of change" favoured Argentina's claim to the islands.

A leaked Pentagon memo from April suggested that Washington could use the Falklands as leverage in negotiations with the UK.

However, the British Foreign Office is understood to be pressing ahead with preparing to announce sanctions on Tuesday.

Miliband released a video late last week in which he said: “I just came out of this meeting talking about Gaza to people who've been there and are there on the ground, and frankly it was horrific what is unfolding.”

He asserted that “we as a UK government, as the prime minister has said, have got to act and act more decisively than we have”.

In response, the official X account of Israel's foreign ministry attacked Miliband and said, "facts matter less (when making a video for a political audience)" to the British foreign secretary.

Mike Huckabee, the US ambassador to Israel, shared the Israeli foreign ministry's post and remarked: "The Brits have lost it. The Jew hate of their government knows no boundaries and knows no facts."

Miliband is Jewish and his parents lost family members in the Holocaust.

title: Israeli strikes kill seven Palestinians in Gaza in past 24 hours
summary:
Israeli strikes kill seven Palestinians in Gaza in past 24 hours

Two Palestinians have died from injuries sustained in Israeli attacks in the Gaza Strip, bringing the number of Palestinians killed over the past 24 hours to seven, according to the Palestinian news agency Wafa. 

Six-year-old Daoud Muqata was killed after being shot north of Gaza City several weeks ago, while Subhi al-Batrikhi succumbed to wounds sustained in an Israeli air attack on a group of civilians in the city’s Remal neighbourhood on Sunday. 

Massive explosions were heard across Gaza around dawn after Israeli air strikes hit residential buildings in Gaza City’s Tuffah neighbourhood, according to local media. 

Israeli jets also struck several locations overnight, including homes belonging to the al-Batsh and Habib families and the Hayfa Hospital building behind the al-Sakhra commercial complex.

title: Iran war shows Gulf cannot rely on US for security, Qatar says
summary:
Iran war shows Gulf cannot rely on US for security, Qatar says

Spokesperson for the Qatari foreign ministry Majed al-Ansari said the war on Iran had shown that Gulf states could no longer rely on strategic alliances with the US for their security. 

Speaking at the Hili Forum in Abu Dhabi, Ansari said the international forces and the US alliance were important but "not enough" to ensure the security of the region.

“We need to realise in the Gulf that having international forces in the region, having a strategic alliance with the US is very important but is not enough. Self-sufficiency when it comes to security is the only way forward,” Ansari said.

Qatar and other Gulf states have condemned Iran's strikes on energy and other infrastructure across the region, saying they violate international law and the UN Charter. 

Alongside Pakistan, Qatar played a key role in brokering an April ceasefire and a June memorandum of understanding between Iran and the US, but both arrangements have since collapsed.

title: Iran says new anti-ship missile was tested over US warship
summary:
Iran says new anti-ship missile was tested over US warship

Iran has successfully tested a new anti-ship missile over a US Navy vessel, said the secretary of the Supreme National Security Council, Major General Mohsen Rezaei, according to Fars News. 

“For the first time, we tested our anti-ship missile above an American warship,” Rezaei said during a televised interview on Sunday night.

 He described the weapon as a “special missile” that “created hell for the Americans”, claiming the US vessels fled the area.

Earlier on Sunday, the Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps said its Aerospace Force had fired several ballistic missiles at a US aircraft carrier and an American destroyer involved in the blockade, forcing the vessels to leave the area, Fars News reported. 

US Central Command has acknowledged that the vessels came under attack by "hostile missiles", adding that they were defeated without damage and were met with retaliatory strikes.

Rezaei said the acknowledgement by US Central Command showed that Washington could not conceal the strikes, calling them a warning that the US naval blockade was vulnerable.
